Ford Targets Certain Japanese Customers With Ranger, F-150, and F-Series Super Duty Pickup Trucks
11 photos
Photo: Ford
Ford intends to push four pickup families onto certain Japanese customers. The Ranger opens the list, followed by the Ranger Super Duty. Higher up the spectrum, the full-size truck segment is represented by the F-150 and F-Series Super Duty, with the latter family stretching from the F-250 to the F-550 workhorse. Ford's global export distributor has appointed Yokohama-based Space Factory as the authorized channel partner in Japan.
Space Factory will bring these vehicles to Japanese government, defense, and humanitarian customers, giving Japanese customers access to a broader Ford truck range than ever before. The Ranger may be perfectly fine over difficult terrain, but an F-550 configured for specialist equipment occupies a very different corner of the market. Ford wants to cover both, and everything in between.
From Japanese ministries to local governments, independent administrative agencies, the Self-Defense Forces, and nongovernmental organizations, there are plenty of prospective customers out there. Their requirements include personnel and equipment transport to remote areas, logistics, disaster relief, and humanitarian operations. Unfortunately, this arrangement is anything but a return to retail sales for the second-largest American automaker after General Motors.
RMA Group-controlled Global Fleet Sales says the Ranger excels over difficult terrain, making it the perfect candidate for organizations that operate in mountainous regions or on remote islands. Being a narrower truck, the mid-sized Ranger is the superior off-road machine in this particular context.
The Super Duty, which wouldn't have been possible without Ford Australia's involvement in the project, is a heavy-duty midsizer developed specifically for clients who need more carrying and towing capacity. Global Fleet Sales lists the Ranger Super Duty with 1,982 kilograms (4,370 pounds) for maximum payload and 4,500 kilograms (9,921 pounds) in terms of maximum towing capacity.
Photo: Ford Australia Those numbers alone make the Ranger Super Duty an interesting pick for agencies that carry specialist equipment. Communications installations, emergency response goodies, and substantial cargo easily eat into the payload capacity of a conventional midsizer. The Super Duty gives clients more headroom while retaining the footprint of a mid-size truck in a country that is widely known for its narrow roads in dense residential and remote mountainous areas.
Stepping up to the F-150 gets you higher payload and towing capacities. In the United States of America, the 2027 model tops 2,440 pounds (1,107 kilograms) and 13,500 pounds (6,124 kilograms), respectively. The big news for 2027 is the canning of the 2.7-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V6 in favor of the 3.0-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V6, a mill that produces a bit more power in the Ranger Raptor.
Above the F-150 sits the Super Duty line, covering a variety of applications. The F-450 with dual rear wheels and the Power Stroke diesel is good for up to 40,000 pounds (18,143 kilograms) when properly equipped, whereas the F-350 with dual rear wheels and the Godzilla naturally aspirated V8 gasser is capable of hauling 7,900 pounds (3,583 kilograms). Importing trucks from the US and Thailand won't satisfy all customers, though.
All targeted clients have different requirements, and that's where RMA Special Vehicles of Thailand enters the picture. This company will provide its vehicle engineering expertise to modify the vehicles as required. Its existing portfolio includes a light tactical vehicle derived from the Ranger Super Duty, utility conversions based on the F-350, and an F-550 oil tanker conversion.
To recap, Global Sales Fleet provides the aforementioned trucks, RMA Special Vehicles does the conversion work, and Space Factory handles servicing in Japan. As of this writing, Global Sales Fleet hasn't confirmed any orders in the Japanese market.
